questions: Why must the probabilities in every discrete distribution sum to exactly 1?
A table lists 0.2, 0.5 and 0.4 - what do you say before doing anything else?
segments.say: A probability table must add to 1. Every discrete distribution lists all its outcomes with their probabilities: here X is 0, 1 or 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3. Watch the three chips travel into the sum - 0.2 plus 0.5 plus 0.3 makes exactly 1, because something has to happen. Make the sum check your reflex for every table in this topic.

questions: Why is the expectation 1.1 even though X can never equal 1.1?
Where would the balance point move if the probability at X = 2 grew?
segments.say: Expectation: the balance point. Expectation is the weighted average E(X) = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) = 1.1. The probe slides along the axis and the fulcrum rises exactly at 1.1: picture the distribution balancing there, and read expectation as the long-run average over many repeats. Check your student notes for the balance-point picture before we count successes.

questions: What are the two halves of the binomial formula, and what goes wrong if either is dropped?
Why does the failure probability 0.7 appear to the power 7 in P(X = 3)?
segments.say: Binomial: n = 10, p = 0.3. Exactly 3 successes in 10 trials means choosing which 3 trials succeed: 10 choose 3 is 120 ways. Each path has probability 0.3 cubed times 0.7 to the 7, so the bar grows to about 0.267. Say the recipe aloud: choose the trials, then price one path. Now open the worksheet and try the binomial question in pairs.

questions: A normal distribution has mean 100 and standard deviation 10 - between which values does about 95% lie?
Why does almost nothing lie beyond three standard deviations from the mean?
segments.say: The 68–95–99.7 rule. The normal curve is pinned down by its mean and standard deviation. Watch the shaded band widen from one sigma to three - covering about 68, then 95, then 99.7 percent of the area. The rule gives instant estimates: mean 100, sigma 10 means about 95% between 80 and 120. Compare the rule's three landmarks in your student notes.

questions: State, in one sentence, why five heads in a row do not make tails due.
In the exit ticket, which question tests independence - and what answer shows you have it?
segments.say: A common mistake: tails is due after five heads. Five heads land one by one, the sixth coin travels in, and the memory needle never moves. Independence means each toss starts fresh: the next toss is 1/2 heads whatever came before. Compare the trap section of your student notes one last time. Now the exit ticket - on your own, no talking - covering the sum check, expectation, the binomial formula and the 68-95-99.7 rule.
segments.watchFor: After five heads in a row, tails is due. Listen and look for it as the exit ticket comes in: any answer pricing tails above 1/2 after the run shows the balancing-out feeling, not independence - send them back to the needle that never moves.
